title: Polar Animals
keyIdea: The Arctic, in the far north, is a frozen ocean with land around it: polar bears, Arctic foxes and walruses live there. The Antarctic, in the far south, is an icy continent with ocean around it: emperor penguins, Weddell seals and albatrosses live there. Polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild. Polar animals are adapted to keep body heat in: blubber (a thick layer of fat), thick fur that traps warm air, small ears, huddling together, and in the Arctic fox a thick white winter coat that turns brown in summer.
familyTip: Try the blubber glove test. Fill a bowl with ice and water. Put a spoonful of lard or butter inside a sandwich bag, and an empty bag next to it. Your child puts one finger in each bag and dips them in the icy water. Which finger stays warm for longer? Ask which polar animals have a layer like that.

visual.caption: Does each animal live in the Arctic or around Antarctica? Drag each card, or tap it then a box.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: send animals to the right pole, thicken a walrus's blubber, huddle penguins, change an Arctic fox's coat, and build a body for a blizzard.

kid: The Arctic is at the top of the world. It is a frozen sea with land around it. Polar bears, Arctic foxes and walruses live there. The Antarctic is at the bottom of the world. It is a big icy land with sea all around. Penguins, Weddell seals and albatrosses live there.
So polar bears and penguins never meet in the wild. Polar bears live only in the north. Penguins live in the south.

Polar animals have adaptations that keep their body heat in. Walruses and seals have blubber, a thick layer of fat under the skin. A polar bear has thick fur too. The fur traps warm air next to its skin. Small ears also help, because less heat escapes.

Emperor penguins huddle close in the winter storms. Each one loses less heat, and they take turns on the cold outside. The Arctic fox grows a thick white coat for winter, so it is hidden in the snow. In summer it turns brown or grey to match the rocks.
adult: Ages 7 to 9. This links the National Curriculum in England for Year 2 (living things and their habitats) with Year 6 (animals are adapted to suit their environment). Key words: Arctic, Antarctic, habitat, adaptation, blubber, insulation, camouflage, moult, huddle.

The Arctic is an ice-covered ocean ringed by North America, Europe and Asia. The Antarctic is a continent under thick ice, ringed by the Southern Ocean. Polar bears, walruses, narwhals and Arctic foxes live only in the north. Penguins live almost only in the southern hemisphere, and none live in the Arctic. Blubber insulates: walrus blubber can be about 15 cm thick, and a polar bear has up to about 11 cm under its thick fur. Fur works by trapping a layer of still air.

Emperor penguins breed in the Antarctic winter. Huddles of thousands cut each bird's heat loss sharply, and birds shuffle so each takes a turn on the windy edge. Arctic foxes have small rounded ears and moult twice a year. Most turn from a thick white winter coat to a thinner brown or grey summer coat; a darker 'blue' form stays dark all year.

Common mistakes: thinking polar bears and penguins live together; thinking blubber is fur or muscle; believing fur makes heat, when it only traps it; saying penguins huddle to hide from polar bears; thinking the Arctic fox is white all year; and expecting big ears to keep an animal warm. In the lab your child sorts six animals to a pole, drags a walrus's blubber thicker until a heat-loss bar turns green, drags six penguins into a huddle, puts the right coat on an Arctic fox in winter and summer, and picks features for a body, then tests it in a blizzard.

choices: only in the Arctic, in the far north
at both the North and South Poles
in Antarctica, with penguins
practice.hint: Polar bears hunt seals on the frozen sea at the top of the world.
practice.explain: Polar bears live only in the Arctic. There are no polar bears in Antarctica, so they never meet penguins in the wild.

choices: a thick layer of fat under the skin
a kind of thick fur
a big muscle for swimming
practice.hint: Walruses and seals have it under their skin, and it keeps heat in.
practice.explain: Blubber is a thick layer of fat under the skin. Body heat passes through it slowly, so the animal stays warm in icy water.

practice.prompt: A huddle has {a} emperor penguins. {b} more shuffle in from the cold. How many penguins are in the huddle now?
practice.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} penguins. The more that huddle, the less heat each one loses.

practice.prompt: A walrus has blubber {w} cm thick. A seal has blubber {s} cm thick. How many cm thicker is the walrus's blubber?
practice.hint: Find the difference: take {s} away from {w}.
practice.explain: {w} − {s} = {=w-s}. The walrus's blubber is {=w-s} cm thicker.

practice.prompt: Why does an Arctic fox have a white coat in winter?
choices: it is hidden against the snow, and the coat is thick and warm
white fur makes heat
it is white all year round
practice.hint: Think about what the ground looks like in winter, and what happens in summer.
practice.explain: A white coat hides the fox on snow, and the winter coat is thick. In summer it moults into a thinner brown or grey coat.

pool.prompt: Why do emperor penguins huddle together in winter?
choices: to share warmth and block the wind
to hide from polar bears
to keep their feathers dry
pool.hint: There are no polar bears in Antarctica. What does standing close do?
pool.explain: Huddling close means less cold wind reaches each penguin, so each one loses less heat. They take turns on the outside.

choices: Weddell seal
walrus
Arctic fox
pool.hint: Two of these live in the far north. One lives in the far south.
pool.explain: Weddell seals live around Antarctica. Walruses and Arctic foxes live in the Arctic.

pool.prompt: How does thick fur keep a polar bear warm?
choices: it traps warm air next to the skin
it makes heat like a heater
it lets the cold out
pool.hint: Fur cannot make heat. What does it hold close to the body?
pool.explain: Fur traps a layer of warm, still air next to the skin, so body heat stays in.

pool.prompt: Zara says big ears keep an Arctic fox warm. What is the mistake?
choices: small ears keep heat in; big ears let heat out
Arctic foxes have no ears
there is no mistake
pool.hint: Compare the desert fennec fox, which needs to lose heat.
pool.explain: The Arctic fox has small rounded ears, so less heat escapes. Big thin ears, like a fennec fox's, let heat out.

pool.prompt: An Arctic fox's winter coat lasts {w} months. Its summer coat lasts the rest of the 12 months. How many months is that?
pool.hint: A year has 12 months. Take away the {w} winter months.

choices: a frozen ocean with land around it, in the far north
an icy continent in the far south
a hot, dry desert
pool.hint: Polar bears walk on its sea ice.
pool.explain: The Arctic is a frozen ocean ringed by land. Antarctica is the icy continent in the south.

pool.prompt: A polar bear swims {a} km one day and {b} km the next. How far does it swim in the two days?
pool.explain: {a} + {b} = {=a+b} km. Thick fur and blubber keep it warm in the icy sea.

pool.prompt: Which set of features best suits an animal in the cold?
choices: thick fur, blubber and small ears
big thin ears and short fur
lots of sweating and thin skin
pool.hint: Choose the features that keep body heat in.
pool.explain: Thick fur, blubber and small ears all keep heat in. Big ears, short fur and sweating let heat escape.
